reason: The sources provide detailed, multi-sourced facts about the discovery, Halloween flyby, physical composition, and skull-like radar appearance of asteroid 2015 TB145.
story: On October 10, 2015, astronomers using the Pan-STARRS telescope in Hawaii discovered a massive space rock racing toward Earth. Just three weeks later, on Halloween day, the object made a safe flyby about 300,000 miles away—just outside the Moon's orbit. When scientists bounced radar signals off the object using the Arecibo Observatory and Goldstone antennas, the returning images revealed an eerie, skull-like shape with dark eye sockets. Data from NASA's Infrared Telescope Facility showed the dark object reflects only six percent of incoming light, similar to fresh asphalt. Lacking a visible coma or tail, astronomers concluded 2015 TB145 was actually a 'dead comet' that had shed its volatile ice after countless passes around the Sun. Travelling at 35 kilometers per second, the spooky celestial visitor safely sped past Earth, leaving behind one of the most haunting astronomical radar images ever captured.
angle: On Halloween 2015, a dead comet shaped remarkably like a human skull flew safely past Earth just beyond the Moon's orbit.

claims.claim: The object was discovered using the Pan-STARRS survey telescope in Hawaii.
The space rock made its close flyby of Earth on Halloween, October 31, 2015.
At closest approach, the object passed about 300,000 miles (480,000 km) from Earth, just outside the Moon's orbit.
Radar images generated by the Arecibo Observatory revealed that the object resembled a human skull.
The object was moving at approximately 35 kilometers per second (78,000 mph) relative to Earth.
Astronomers concluded the object is likely a dead comet that lost its volatile ice after orbiting the Sun repeatedly.
The object reflects only about 6 percent of the sunlight it receives, comparable to fresh asphalt.
The object completes one full rotation on its axis approximately every five hours.
Radar imaging techniques achieved spatial resolution down to 2 meters per pixel.
At peak brightness, the asteroid reached an apparent magnitude of around 10, requiring a small telescope to see.
The next known flyby of an object this size coming this close to Earth will occur in August 2027 with asteroid 1999 AN10.
2015 TB145 made another, much more distant flyby past Earth in late 2018.
The object was discovered only about three weeks before its closest approach to Earth.

disputed: Object diameter estimates vary between sources, ranging from 400 meters (1,300 feet) to 650 meters (2,000 feet); scripts should state the range as roughly 1,300 to 2,000 feet wide.
Media nicknames vary across reports (e.g., 'Great Pumpkin', 'Spooky', 'Death Comet', 'Skull Asteroid'); scripts should frame these explicitly as popular media nicknames.
